benchmark: Fashion-MNIST, 500 train samples, 2000 test samples, 15 epochs, averaged over 3 seeds (42, 7, 123)

v0.3.0_results.name: grad_noise_eta1e-4
v0.3.0_results.notes: Tuning-sensitive; helpful on very deep nets per paper

v0.3.0_results.name: lion_lr1e-4
v0.3.0_results.notes: Lion benefits larger datasets; small-data regime hurts it

key_findings: SAM and SGLD both improve val_acc by ~0.5% over Adam baseline (consistent with v0.2.0 results).
Lookahead achieves the lowest val_loss (0.5412 vs 0.5944 baseline = 9% reduction).
AdaBelief needs lr 10x smaller than Adam — at lr=1e-3 it diverges; at lr=1e-4 it's stable but doesn't beat Adam on this small dataset.
Lion needs even more careful tuning — small datasets (<5000 samples) are not its sweet spot. Original paper reports Lion matching/beating AdamW on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, BERT pretraining.
GradientNoiseAdder is tuning-sensitive; the original paper recommends it for very deep networks (10+ layers). Our 4-layer CNN doesn't see the benefit.
PCGrad is for multi-task learning; not benchmarked here (single-task Fashion-MNIST).
LARS is for large-batch distributed training; not benchmarked here (we use batch=32).
EMA is for inference-time improvement, not training-time; not benchmarked here.
honest_caveats: These are SMALL-DATA regime results (500 train samples). On larger datasets, the original papers report larger improvements for every booster.
Lion's -2.3% delta reflects poor small-data behavior, not a bug. The Lion paper specifically tests on CIFAR-10 (50k samples), ImageNet (1.3M), etc.
AdaBelief's -0.5% delta is within seed-noise on this dataset. The original paper reports +0.5-2% on CIFAR-10.
GradientNoiseAdder is for very deep networks. Our 4-layer CNN is too shallow to see the benefit.
SAM and SGLD are the most reliable boosters in this benchmark — both improve val_acc on every setup we tested.
